headline: Bunker schools pack the beachfront — bluefish keep the rods bent while fluke go quiet in the heat
subhead: Blues are the story from Island Beach to the Barnegat Light rocks while summer fluke settle into their usual sulk on the channel edges.
body_markdown:
I remember a July back in the early '90s when my old mate Sal Petrone and I ran the skiff out past the Coast Guard station at Barnegat Light and hit a bunker school so thick you could've walked across it. Blues came up under it like the bay itself was boiling, and we filled the cooler in twenty minutes without ever putting a line more than three feet down. I think about that morning every time this pattern sets up again — and it's set up again right now, same as it has for weeks. We said it last week and it's still true: the bluefish are the headline on this bay, and they're not giving up the spot.

Water's sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s in the shallows, low 70s out toward the inlet mouth where the ocean water mixes in on the tide. That kind of warm has pushed the bunker schools up tight against the beachfront — Island Beach State Park, the surf line off Barnegat Light, and inside the bay wherever there's current pulling bait past a point. The blues have been on them relentlessly. I had a report from a guy running out of the Oyster Creek launch who hit a blitz right off the north end of the park Tuesday morning — blues to six, seven pounds crashing peanut bunker so hard the water looked like it was under a hailstorm. Chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig will get bit, but if you want the real fun, throw poppers or Hopkins spoons right into the melee. No finesse needed. They're not fussy when they're feeding like that.

Inside the bay, the bluefish have been working the mouth of Double Creek Channel and up around Tices Shoal on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing — that current line where the channel water meets the flat holds bait, and the blues stack up on the edge waiting for it to get pushed to them. Bunker chunks or a white bucktail with a strip of belly meat has been the ticket there. Bring a wire leader or expect to lose gear — these fish are toothy and they don't care that it's July.

Fluke are a different conversation, and I'll be honest with you — it's been a grind. Same story every summer once the shallow water heats up like this: shorts everywhere, keepers scarce unless you go looking for them in the right spots. I've been working the deeper edges of Double Creek Channel, 12 to 15 feet, and around the humps off the Oyster Creek mouth where there's still some cooler water moving through on a strong tide. Best window has been the two hours around the top of the high, when the current's still got some push but hasn't gone full ripping yet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along bottom, have out-produced bait rigs for me this week — the softer plastic seems to draw more strikes when the fish are a little lazy in the warm water. Keepers have been coming, but you're earning them, not stumbling into them. I'd guess for every legal fluke we're throwing back four or five shorts.

Striped bass have gone quiet in daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down the whole coast right now — warm surface water's pushed them down and nocturnal. If you want bass on this bay in July, you fish the dark. I've had better luck working the deeper holes off Barnegat Light on the outgoing tide starting an hour before sunset, live eels or bunker chunks fished on bottom. Nothing fast, but there's still fish there if you're patient and willing to be out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m.

Weakfish have been sparse on our end of things — not the story it apparently is down in Delaware Bay right now. I haven't heard of anything worth chasing at the sedges this week, which is unusual for late July, but the water's been so warm that I suspect what weakfish we do have have pushed into deeper, cooler pockets and gone quiet like everything else that isn't a bluefish.

Blowfish and kingfish are still around for the bait guys — sandworms and squid strips fished on high-low rigs off the bay bottom near Forked River and up toward Toms River have been steady for blowfish, nothing spectacular but consistent enough to keep the kids in the boat entertained.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to break. The wind's been stable, the bunker schools show no sign of thinning out, and warm water isn't going anywhere with this weather holding. I'd expect the blue­fish blitz to keep working its way along the beachfront and into the bay mouths through the weekend — that's still the most reliable card on the table. If you want fluke, go early, go deep, and be patient on the channel edges. If you want bass, set your alarm for late and fish the dark water off the inlet structure. And if the bunker schools ever thin out or a stiff northeast blow scatters them, that bluefish window will close fast — so if you've got a morning free this week, I wouldn't wait on it.
